sections.heading: Food gives us more than energy

sections.heading: Simple tests for nutrients
sections.body: Iodine solution turns blue-black with starch. Copper sulphate and caustic soda produce a violet colour with protein. A translucent spot on paper suggests fat. These simple tests help us understand what our food contains.

sections.heading: Plants make their own food
sections.body: Green plants make food through photosynthesis. Leaves contain chlorophyll, a green pigment that captures sunlight. The plant takes carbon dioxide from the air through tiny openings called stomata and water from the soil through roots. Sunlight provides energy to combine these into glucose, and oxygen is released.
bullets: Carbon dioxide + water + sunlight → glucose + oxygen.
Chlorophyll is found inside chloroplasts.
Photosynthesis happens mainly in leaves.

sections.heading: Adaptations for photosynthesis
sections.body: Leaves are broad and flat to capture light, thin so gases diffuse easily, and have veins that carry water and glucose. Stomata open and close to balance gas exchange with water loss. Plants in bright sunlight may grow leaves at different angles to avoid overheating.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: Photosynthesis produces the food at the base of almost every food chain. It also releases the oxygen we breathe. Protecting trees and green cover protects both food and air. In a village, shade trees and crop plants are part of the same global process.

definitions.meaning: The process by which green plants use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make food.
The green pigment in leaves that absorbs light energy.
Tiny openings on leaves that let gases enter and leave.

notes: Photosynthesis needs light, chlorophyll, carbon dioxide and water.
Oxygen is a by-product, not the main goal for the plant.
At night, plants respire and take in oxygen.

examples.title: Potted plant near a window

examples.title: Crop field
examples.description: Healthy green leaves capture more sunlight and produce a better yield.

applications: Farmers manage spacing so each plant receives enough light.
Forests cool the air and release oxygen through photosynthesis.
keyPoints: Plants are autotrophs: they make their own food.
Chlorophyll captures light energy.
Water and carbon dioxide are the raw materials.
Oxygen is released during the process.
Photosynthesis supports nearly all food chains.

practiceQuestions.answer: To capture as much sunlight as possible.

practiceQuestions.answer: It stops because there is no sunlight; respiration continues.

sections.heading: What is a rational number?
sections.body: A rational number is any number that can be written as p/q, where p and q are integers and q is not zero. Examples include 3/4, -5/7, 6 (because 6 = 6/1) and 0 (0/1). Rational numbers include integers, terminating decimals and repeating decimals.
bullets: Every integer is a rational number.
0 is a rational number, but division by 0 is undefined.
The same rational number has many equivalent forms, such as 1/2 = 2/4 = 50/100.

sections.heading: Placing them on the number line
sections.body: Rational numbers fill the spaces between integers. To place 3/4, divide the gap between 0 and 1 into four equal parts and count three parts. Negative rationals sit to the left of zero. Between any two rational numbers you can always find another rational number — for example, the average of 1/3 and 1/2 is 5/12.

sections.heading: Working with rational numbers
sections.body: To add or subtract, write both numbers with a common denominator. To multiply, multiply numerators and denominators. To divide, multiply by the reciprocal. Always simplify the answer and keep the sign with the numerator. For example: 2/3 + 1/4 = 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.

definitions.meaning: A number that can be written as p/q where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0.
The number obtained by swapping numerator and denominator; 3/5 and 5/3 are reciprocals.
The number 0, because adding 0 does not change a number.

notes: A rational number has a terminating or repeating decimal expansion.
Division by zero is not allowed.
Keep answers in simplest form.

examples.title: Temperature change

applications: Recipes use fractions such as 1/2 cup or 3/4 teaspoon.

keyPoints: Rational numbers are of the form p/q, q ≠ 0.
Integers and terminating decimals are rational.
Common denominators make addition and subtraction easy.
Multiplying by the reciprocal performs division.
There are infinitely many rational numbers between any two rational numbers.

practiceQuestions.question: Is 0.75 rational? Explain.
practiceQuestions.answer: Yes. 0.75 = 75/100 = 3/4, which is in p/q form.

sections.heading: Preparing the soil
sections.body: Farmers prepare land before sowing. Ploughing loosens and turns the soil, bringing nutrients to the surface and letting air and water enter. Wooden or iron ploughs are pulled by animals or tractors. After ploughing, the field is levelled so that water stays evenly distributed and seeds are sown at a similar depth.
bullets: Ploughing improves air circulation in the soil.
Levelling prevents water from collecting in low patches.
Manure and compost add organic matter and improve soil texture.

sections.heading: Choosing and sowing seeds
sections.body: Good seeds are healthy, clean, uniform in size and free from damage. Farmers sometimes soak seeds in water to test which ones are viable — healthy seeds sink. Sowing can be done by hand, by a seed drill, or by transplanting seedlings. The right spacing gives each plant enough sunlight, water and nutrients.

sections.heading: Caring for the crop
sections.body: Crops need water at the right times. Irrigation may come from canals, wells, tube wells, ponds or rainwater harvesting. Weeds compete with crops for water and nutrients, so they are removed by hand, with a hoe, or with weedicides used carefully. Pests and diseases are controlled through observation, resistant varieties and safe practices.

definitions.meaning: Loosening and turning the soil to prepare it for sowing.

Removing unwanted plants that compete with the crop.
A tool that sows seeds at a uniform depth and spacing.

notes: Healthy seeds sink in water; damaged or hollow seeds float.

sections.heading: What is electric current?
sections.body: Electric current is the flow of electric charge through a material. In the wires of a circuit, tiny particles called electrons drift along the wire when a cell or battery pushes them. We measure current in amperes (A) and often use the symbol I. A current needs a complete path, called a closed circuit, before it can flow.
bullets: A cell has a positive terminal and a negative terminal.
Current flows only when the circuit is closed, with no gaps.
A switch is simply a controlled gap that opens or closes the circuit.

sections.heading: How a bulb lights up
sections.body: Inside a torch bulb there is a thin tungsten filament. When current passes through it, the filament resists the flow and becomes very hot. It glows and gives out light. The glass bulb protects the filament and keeps oxygen away so it does not burn quickly. If the filament breaks, the circuit is open and the bulb stops glowing.
bullets: The filament's high resistance converts electrical energy into heat and light.
Two terminals at the base of the bulb connect to the circuit.

sections.heading: Cells, batteries and safe circuits
sections.body: A cell stores chemical energy and changes it into electrical energy. A battery is a group of cells joined together. In school experiments we use low-voltage cells and never connect the two terminals directly with a wire — that is a short circuit. It makes wires hot and can damage the cell or cause a fire.

definitions.meaning: The flow of electric charge through a conductor, measured in amperes (A).
A complete closed path through which electric current can flow.
The thin high-resistance wire inside a bulb that glows when current passes.
A device that opens or closes a circuit to control current.

notes: Draw every circuit as a clean diagram with symbols: cell, switch, bulb and connecting wires.
An open circuit has a gap, so current cannot flow and the bulb does not glow.
Never experiment with mains electricity (220 V). Use cells or batteries only.

sections.heading: Light travels in straight lines
sections.body: Light is a form of energy that lets us see. It travels in straight lines until it meets a surface. When light hits a smooth, shiny surface such as a plane mirror, it bounces back. This bouncing is called reflection. The ray that arrives is the incident ray, and the ray that leaves is the reflected ray.
bullets: The normal is a line perpendicular to the mirror at the point where light hits.
Angle of incidence is measured between the incident ray and the normal.
Angle of reflection is measured between the reflected ray and the normal.

sections.heading: Laws of reflection
sections.body: The angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection. The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal all lie in the same plane. In a plane mirror the image is virtual, behind the mirror, the same size as the object, and left–right reversed. The image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it.

sections.heading: Seeing objects
sections.body: We see a book because light from the sun or a bulb falls on it and scatters into our eyes. We see an image in a mirror because reflected rays reach our eyes. In a completely dark room no light enters our eyes from objects, so we cannot see them — even though our eyes are open.

definitions.meaning: The bouncing back of light when it hits a surface.
A line drawn perpendicular to a surface at the point of incidence.
An image from which light rays only appear to come; it cannot be caught on a screen.

notes: Always draw the normal as a dotted line.
Plane mirrors produce virtual, erect images of the same size.
Diffuse reflection from rough surfaces lets us see ordinary objects from many directions.

keyPoints: Light travels in straight lines.
Angle of incidence = angle of reflection.
A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect, same-size image.
Rough surfaces scatter light, which is called diffuse reflection.
We see non-luminous objects only when light from them reaches our eyes.

practiceQuestions.question: Why can you see your face in a mirror but not in a mud wall?
practiceQuestions.answer: A mirror has a smooth surface and reflects light in a regular way. A mud wall has a rough surface and scatters light in many directions.

practiceQuestions.answer: 1) Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection. 2) The incident ray, normal and reflected ray lie in the same plane.

sections.heading: The story within the story
sections.body: The narrator visits an old house and finds a letter hidden in a desk. The letter tells of Jim Macpherson, a soldier in the First World War, and his wife Connie. Jim writes about a Christmas truce when soldiers from opposite sides stopped fighting, shared food and played football. The reader moves between the narrator's present and Jim's past.

sections.heading: Theme: peace and kindness
sections.body: The story asks what war does to ordinary people and how small acts of kindness survive inside it. Jim's letter is a gift of memory. When the narrator meets Connie, she believes her husband has returned; the story ends with tenderness rather than correction. The Christmas present is not an object — it is the message that humanity can still be found in terrible times.

sections.heading: Tense and time
sections.body: Tense tells us when an action happens. Simple present describes habits and facts: I walk to school. Present continuous describes actions happening now: I am walking. Present perfect connects the past to now: I have finished my homework. Simple past describes completed past actions, and simple future describes what will happen.
bullets: Use time markers such as now, yesterday, already and next week.
Keep the tense consistent inside a paragraph unless the time changes.
Irregular verbs have special past forms: go → went, write → wrote.

sections.heading: Choosing the right tense
sections.body: Ask: when did the action happen, and is it finished? For a school trip last week, use simple past. For a habit, use simple present. For an action that started in the past and still matters now, use present perfect. Sentences like 'I have visited Nabha last year' are wrong because 'last year' points to a finished time; say 'I visited Nabha last year.'

notes: Present perfect = have/has + past participle.

sections.heading: A rulebook for the nation
sections.body: The Constitution is the highest law of India. It was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950. It explains how the government is formed, what powers it has, and what rights every person holds. No ordinary law can violate the Constitution.

sections.heading: Federalism and separation of powers
sections.body: India has a federal system with a central government and state governments. Powers are divided by lists: Union, State and Concurrent. The Constitution also separates the legislature, executive and judiciary so that no single branch becomes too powerful. Courts can review whether laws follow the Constitution.

sections.heading: Fundamental rights and equality
sections.body: Fundamental rights protect equality, freedom, life, education and protection from exploitation. They are enforceable in court. Rights come with responsibilities, and reasonable restrictions can be placed on them to protect public order and safety. The Constitution also names duties that guide citizens.

definitions.meaning: The fundamental law that sets out the structure and powers of government and the rights of citizens.
A system where power is shared between national and state governments.
Basic rights guaranteed by the Constitution and protected by courts.

notes: 26 January is celebrated as Republic Day.
Dr B. R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee.
Fundamental rights apply to every person in India, not only citizens.

examples.title: Right to Education
examples.description: Children aged 6–14 have a constitutional right to free and compulsory education.

examples.title: Equality before law
examples.description: The same law applies to every citizen, whatever their background.

applications: Knowing your rights helps you respond to unfair treatment.
Village committees and panchayats operate within constitutional rules.
keyPoints: The Constitution is the supreme law.
It was adopted in 1949 and enforced in 1950.
Federalism shares power between the Union and states.
Fundamental rights protect individuals and are enforceable.
Rights and duties go together.

practiceQuestions.question: Why is the Constitution called the supreme law?
practiceQuestions.answer: All other laws and government actions must follow it; courts can strike down laws that violate it.

practiceQuestions.question: Name two fundamental rights.
practiceQuestions.answer: The right to equality and the right to education (other valid answers include freedom, life and protection from exploitation).

sections.heading: Particles in three states
sections.body: Matter is made of tiny particles with spaces between them and motion of their own. In solids, particles are tightly packed and vibrate in place, so solids have fixed shape and volume. In liquids, particles are close but can slide, so liquids flow and take the shape of the container. In gases, particles are far apart and move quickly, filling any container.
bullets: Solids: fixed shape and volume.
Liquids: fixed volume, take container shape.
Gases: no fixed shape or volume, highly compressible.

sections.heading: Evidence from everyday life
sections.body: A drop of ink spreads in water without stirring because particles move and mix. The smell of incense travels across a room. Gases compress easily in a syringe, while a solid brick does not. These observations support the particle model of matter.

sections.heading: Temperature and particle motion
sections.body: Heating increases the kinetic energy of particles. At a certain temperature, a solid melts and a liquid boils. Cooling removes energy and slows particles, allowing a gas to condense and a liquid to freeze. The temperature remains steady during a change of state because energy is used to break or form attractions rather than raise temperature.

definitions.meaning: The spreading of particles from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration.

notes: Particles are always in motion, even in solids.

sections.heading: What makes an equation quadratic?
sections.body: A quadratic equation has the form ax² + bx + c = 0, where a ≠ 0. The highest power of the variable is 2. Examples include x² − 5x + 6 = 0 and 2x² + 3x − 2 = 0. Its solutions are called roots, and a quadratic has at most two real roots.

sections.heading: Factorisation
sections.body: To solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0, find two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to −5: −2 and −3. Split the middle term, group and factor: (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0. So x = 2 or x = 3. Always set each factor to zero, never just one.

sections.heading: Formula and discriminant
sections.body: When factorisation is difficult, use x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a. The discriminant D = b² − 4ac tells us the nature of the roots: D > 0 gives two distinct real roots, D = 0 gives equal roots, and D < 0 gives no real roots. Check answers by substituting them back into the equation.

b² − 4ac, which determines the nature of the roots.

notes: Set the equation to zero before factorising.

sections.heading: The three quantities
sections.body: Electric current (I) is the rate of flow of charge and is measured in amperes. Potential difference (V) is the work done to move a unit charge between two points and is measured in volts. Resistance (R) opposes the flow of current and is measured in ohms. Ohm's law connects them: V = IR at constant temperature.

sections.heading: Understanding resistance
sections.body: A long, thin wire has more resistance than a short, thick one. Resistance depends on the material, length, thickness and temperature. Resistors are used to control current in circuits. A voltmeter is connected in parallel to measure potential difference, while an ammeter is connected in series to measure current.

sections.heading: Using Ohm's law
sections.body: If a 6 V battery is connected across a 3 Ω resistor, the current is I = V/R = 2 A. Ohm's law works for metallic conductors at constant temperature. Filament bulbs do not obey it exactly because their temperature changes, but the law remains a useful starting point.

exploreContents.title: How does electricity reach our homes?
exploreContents.shortDescription: Follow the journey of electricity from a power station to the switch on your wall.

sections.heading: Generation
sections.body: Electricity is generated in power stations. In Punjab, thermal plants burn fuel, hydro plants use falling water, and solar farms convert sunlight. A generator produces alternating current by turning a coil inside a magnetic field.
bullets: Thermal, hydro, wind and solar all feed the same grid.
The voltage is raised before transmission to reduce energy loss.

sections.heading: Transmission and distribution
sections.body: High-voltage lines carry electricity across long distances. Substations lower the voltage step by step. Distribution transformers bring it to a safe level for homes, and service wires connect to your electricity meter.
bullets: High voltage reduces current for the same power, so wires waste less energy.
The meter records how much energy your home uses.

sections.heading: Inside the house
sections.body: Live, neutral and earth wires work together. The live wire carries current, the neutral completes the path, and the earth wire protects people if a metal casing becomes live. A switch opens the circuit so an appliance stops drawing current.

definitions.meaning: A device that increases or decreases alternating voltage.
The connected network of generation, transmission and distribution.

practicalExamples: A ceiling fan stops when its switch opens the circuit.
A fuse melts before a faulty appliance can overheat.
keyTakeaways: Generation, transmission and distribution are separate stages.
Transformers change voltage safely.
Earth wires and fuses protect people.

exploreContents.title: How do solar panels generate electricity?
exploreContents.shortDescription: Sunlight becomes electricity inside a silent, moving-part-free panel.

sections.heading: The photovoltaic effect
sections.body: A solar panel is made of many solar cells. Each cell has layers of silicon treated to have different electrical properties. When photons from sunlight strike the cell, they free electrons. The built-in electric field pushes those electrons in one direction, creating current.
bullets: Only sunlight, not heat alone, drives the photovoltaic effect.
Cells are connected in series to raise voltage.

sections.heading: From panel to appliance
sections.body: Panels produce direct current (DC). An inverter converts it to alternating current (AC) for household appliances. A charge controller protects a battery in off-grid systems, and net metering lets surplus power flow back to the grid.

sections.heading: Why it suits rural homes
sections.body: Solar pumps, lanterns and rooftop systems work without a diesel supply and need little maintenance. Panels produce most power around midday, so batteries or grid backup are needed for evening use. Dust reduces output, so regular cleaning matters.

definitions.meaning: The production of voltage when light strikes a material.
A device that changes DC into AC.

practicalExamples: A solar pump lifts drinking water during the day.
A rooftop system charges batteries for evening lights.
keyTakeaways: Sunlight frees electrons in silicon cells.
Inverters make panel output usable at home.
Batteries store energy for later.

exploreContents.title: How does the internet work?
exploreContents.shortDescription: A request from your phone travels through networks and comes back with a web page.

sections.heading: Networks talking to networks
sections.body: The internet is a network of networks. Your phone connects to a router, which connects to your internet service provider. Data is broken into packets, each labelled with a destination address, and routers pass packets along the best available path.
bullets: Packets may travel different routes and are reassembled at the destination.
IP addresses identify devices; DNS translates names like example.com into addresses.

sections.heading: Request and response
sections.body: When you open a website, your browser sends an HTTP request to a server. The server responds with HTML, CSS, JavaScript and images. HTTPS encrypts this exchange so that others on the network cannot read or change it.
bullets: A web server listens for requests on a port.
Caching stores copies closer to you so pages load faster.

sections.heading: What this means for you
sections.body: Data travels over wires, optical fibre and mobile radio links. Distance and congestion affect speed. A weak mobile signal means more retransmissions and slower loading. This is why NabhaLearn keeps pages lightweight and avoids unnecessary downloads.

definitions.meaning: A small unit of data sent across a network.
The system that maps domain names to IP addresses.
Encrypted HTTP that protects data in transit.

practicalExamples: A video call sends and receives packets continuously.
A school computer loads a website through a local router.
keyTakeaways: The internet is a network of networks.
Data travels as packets using IP addresses.
HTTPS encrypts browser traffic.
Caching and lightweight pages improve slow connections.

exploreContents.title: How does a refrigerator work?
exploreContents.shortDescription: A fridge moves heat from inside to outside using evaporation and condensation.

sections.heading: Moving heat, not making cold
sections.body: A refrigerator does not create cold. It removes heat from the food compartment and releases it at the back. A refrigerant flows through a closed loop, changing between liquid and gas as it moves.
bullets: Evaporation absorbs heat.
Condensation releases heat.

sections.heading: The four parts
sections.body: The compressor raises the pressure and temperature of the refrigerant gas. In the condenser coils at the back, the gas releases heat and becomes liquid. The expansion valve lowers the pressure, and the evaporator inside the fridge lets the liquid absorb heat and turn back into gas.

sections.heading: Using a fridge well
sections.body: Keep the door closed, leave space for air to circulate and never block the back coils. A fridge works harder in a hot room. Defrosting and cleaning door seals reduce electricity use.

definitions.meaning: A fluid that absorbs and releases heat as it changes state.
A pump that raises refrigerant pressure.

practicalExamples: The back of a fridge feels warm because it releases heat.
A pressure cooker and a fridge both use pressure changes.
keyTakeaways: A fridge moves heat outside.
Evaporation absorbs heat; condensation releases it.
Good habits reduce electricity use.

exploreContents.title: How do farmers use modern technology?
exploreContents.shortDescription: From soil testing to drip irrigation, technology helps farmers save water and grow more.

sections.heading: Better decisions before sowing
sections.body: Soil testing measures nutrients and pH so farmers can add the right amount of fertiliser. Weather forecasts guide sowing dates. Certified seed varieties resist disease and give predictable yields.
bullets: Over-fertilising wastes money and harms soil.
Seed treatment protects young plants.

sections.heading: Water and crop care
sections.body: Drip and sprinkler irrigation deliver water directly where it is needed, saving both water and labour. Soil moisture sensors tell farmers when to irrigate. Drones and phone apps can help spot pest outbreaks early, though they are not available to every farmer yet.

sections.heading: Harvest, storage and market
sections.body: Combine harvesters speed up harvesting. Clean, dry storage limits mould. Mobile messages and online market platforms help farmers compare prices. Solar dryers preserve vegetables and fruit so less produce is wasted.

definitions.meaning: A system that delivers water drop by drop near plant roots.
A laboratory check of soil nutrients and pH.

practicalExamples: A farmer uses a soil test to choose fertiliser.
A solar dryer preserves vegetables for off-season sale.
keyTakeaways: Technology supports decisions, not just machines.
Water-saving irrigation protects a shared resource.
Storage and market information reduce losses.

exploreContents.title: How does a water pump work?
exploreContents.shortDescription: A pump uses pressure differences to lift water from a well or borewell.

sections.heading: Creating a pressure difference
sections.body: A pump does not 'suck' water in the way we often say. It lowers the pressure at its inlet, and atmospheric pressure pushes water up into the pipe. Then the pump pushes the water out. The maximum practical lift is limited by atmospheric pressure and friction.
bullets: Pumps must be primed before they can move water.
Air leaks in a suction pipe stop water from rising.

sections.heading: Common pump types
sections.body: A hand pump uses a piston and valves. A centrifugal pump spins an impeller that throws water outward, creating flow. A submersible pump sits inside a borewell and pushes water upward. Solar pumps use panels to run a motor without diesel.

sections.heading: Care and efficiency
sections.body: Keep intake screens clean. Avoid running a pump dry. Match the pump size to the depth and required flow. A leaking pipe can waste more water than the pump can supply, so check joints regularly.

definitions.meaning: Filling a pump and suction pipe with water before starting.
A rotating part that moves water in a centrifugal pump.

practicalExamples: A hand pump lifts water using a piston.
A solar submersible pump fills a tank in a village.
keyTakeaways: Atmospheric pressure helps lift water.
Different pumps suit different depths and uses.
Maintenance and pipe checks save water.

exploreContents.title: Why does the Moon change shape?
exploreContents.shortDescription: The Moon does not change. We see different amounts of its sunlit side as it orbits Earth.

sections.heading: A half-lit sphere in space
sections.body: The Moon has no light of its own; it reflects sunlight. At any moment half of the Moon is lit and half is dark. As the Moon orbits Earth, we see different portions of the lit half, producing phases from new moon to full moon.

sections.heading: The monthly cycle
sections.body: A full cycle takes about 29.5 days. Starting from new moon, the crescent grows (waxing) to first quarter, then full moon. It then shrinks (wanes) through last quarter back to new moon. The phases are not caused by Earth's shadow — that causes eclipses, which are less frequent.

sections.heading: Observing from Nabha
sections.body: The Moon rises at different times depending on its phase. A full moon rises near sunset and sets near sunrise. Keeping a simple drawing log for a month is an excellent astronomy project.

definitions.meaning: The visible portion of the Moon's sunlit side from Earth.
Growing from new moon toward full moon.

practicalExamples: A full moon rising at sunset.
A thin crescent visible just after sunset.
keyTakeaways: The Moon reflects sunlight.
Phases come from our changing viewing angle.
One cycle takes about a month.

exploreContents.title: How do trees help a village?
exploreContents.shortDescription: Trees cool air, hold soil, recharge water and support food and livelihoods.

sections.heading: Shade and cooler air
sections.body: Trees release water vapour through transpiration, which cools the air around them. Their canopy blocks direct sunlight. A shaded street can be several degrees cooler than an open one.

sections.heading: Soil and water
sections.body: Roots hold soil in place during rain, reducing erosion. Leaf litter and roots help rain soak into the ground instead of running off, supporting groundwater recharge. A small planted patch can protect a village pond's bank.

sections.heading: Food, income and habitat
sections.body: Trees provide fruit, fodder, fuel and timber, and they shelter birds and insects. Native species need less water and support more local wildlife. Planting the right tree in the right place matters more than planting many random saplings.

definitions.meaning: Loss of water vapour from plant leaves.
Movement of surface water into underground stores.

practicalExamples: Neem and peepal trees give shade and habitat.
Contour planting on a slope slows runoff.
keyTakeaways: Trees cool and clean the environment.
Roots reduce erosion and help recharge water.
Native species are easier to sustain.

exploreContents.title: Why do we have time zones?
exploreContents.shortDescription: Earth spins, so noon arrives at different places at different moments.

sections.heading: A spinning planet
sections.body: Earth rotates once in about 24 hours, so the Sun appears to move across the sky. When it is noon in one place, it may be morning or evening elsewhere. Time zones give neighbouring regions a shared clock.

sections.heading: How zones are drawn
sections.body: The world is roughly divided into 24 zones, each about 15 degrees of longitude wide. India follows a single time, IST (UTC+5:30), even though the country spans a wide longitude range. The half-hour offset keeps the whole country on one clock.

sections.heading: Why the half hour
sections.body: India's standard meridian is 82.5°E, which gives a 5.5-hour offset from UTC. One national time simplifies railways, exams and business, even though sunrise in the east occurs earlier than in the west.

definitions.meaning: Coordinated Universal Time, the reference for world clocks.
The longitude chosen for a region's official time.

practicalExamples: A train timetable uses one national time.
A call to another country needs a time-zone check.
keyTakeaways: Time zones follow Earth's rotation.
Most zones are one hour apart.
India uses one time with a half-hour offset.

exploreContents.title: How to keep drinking water safe at home
exploreContents.shortDescription: Simple habits — boiling, filtering and clean storage — prevent water-borne illness.

sections.heading: Make water safe
sections.body: Boiling water for at least one minute kills most germs. Filtering removes mud and some contaminants, but a filter alone may not remove all microbes. Chlorination tablets are useful when boiling is not possible, if used exactly as directed.

sections.heading: Store it cleanly
sections.body: Use a covered container with a tap or a clean ladle. Never dip dirty hands or cups into stored water. Clean the container regularly and keep it off the floor. Even safe water can become unsafe through careless storage.

sections.heading: Protect the source
sections.body: Keep hand pumps and wells away from toilets and animal waste. Repair leaks, cover open wells and avoid dumping waste near a water source. Handwashing with soap remains one of the most effective health habits.

definitions.meaning: The presence of harmful germs or chemicals in water.
Adding a measured amount of chlorine to disinfect water.

practicalExamples: Boiling water and cooling it covered.
Using a ladle instead of a cup to take water.
keyTakeaways: Boiling is a reliable way to kill germs.
Clean storage is as important as treatment.
Protect water sources from waste.

exploreContents.title: Careers around agriculture and food science
exploreContents.shortDescription: Farming is one part of a large chain of science, business and technology careers.

sections.heading: Science and technology roles
sections.body: Agricultural scientists study soil, seeds and pests. Food technologists develop safe packaged foods. Agricultural engineers design irrigation and farm machinery. Veterinary doctors keep animals healthy. These roles usually need a degree or diploma after Class 12.

sections.heading: Business and services
sections.body: Agri-business managers buy, store and sell produce. Rural bankers help farmers plan loans. Supply-chain coordinators move food from farms to markets. Many of these careers combine agriculture knowledge with commerce or management.

sections.heading: Building a path from school
sections.body: Focus on science and mathematics, practise careful observation and learn to use spreadsheets. Talk to local farmers, visit a soil-testing lab and join a school gardening project. Ask your teachers about diploma courses and scholarships rather than relying on rumour.

definitions.meaning: The science of crop production and soil management.
The study of processing, preserving and packaging food safely.

practicalExamples: A soil-testing officer advises farmers.
A food technologist checks packaged food safety.
keyTakeaways: Agriculture connects many careers.
Science, commerce and management all apply.
Practical projects and clear information help career choices.

exploreContents.title: Five surprising facts about sound
exploreContents.shortDescription: Sound is a vibration that needs a medium — and it can do some very strange things.

sections.heading: Sound needs a medium
sections.body: Sound travels as a wave of vibrating particles. It cannot travel through a vacuum because there are no particles to carry the vibration. This is why space is silent, even though films often add dramatic explosions.

sections.heading: Speed depends on the material
sections.body: Sound travels faster in water than in air, and faster still in steel. Particles are packed closer together, so vibrations pass along more quickly. The speed of sound in air is about 343 m/s at room temperature.

sections.heading: Pitch, loudness and echoes
sections.body: Pitch depends on frequency, and loudness depends on amplitude. An echo is a reflected sound. Bats use echoes to navigate, and ultrasound scanners use high-frequency sound to see inside the body.

definitions.meaning: The number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz.
A sound heard again after reflection from a surface.

practicalExamples: Hearing an echo in a large hall.
Bats locating insects using ultrasound.
keyTakeaways: Sound needs a medium.
Sound travels faster in denser media.
Frequency controls pitch.

exploreContents.title: How did Newton study motion?
exploreContents.shortDescription: The famous apple story is only a hint. Newton built a system that explained falling and orbiting.

sections.heading: The question
sections.body: Newton asked whether the force that pulls an apple to the ground could also be the force that keeps the Moon in orbit. Instead of treating these as separate phenomena, he looked for one rule that explained both.

sections.heading: From observation to mathematics
sections.body: Newton used observations and mathematics to show that gravitational force depends on mass and distance. His laws of motion connected force, mass and acceleration. These ideas unified falling objects and planetary orbits under a single framework.

sections.heading: How science really works
sections.body: The apple story is often simplified. Newton built on work by Galileo, Kepler and others, and his ideas were debated and tested. Science advances through observation, mathematics, criticism and repeated testing — not a single moment of inspiration.

definitions.meaning: The attractive force between objects with mass.
An object's tendency to resist a change in motion.

practicalExamples: A ball falls to the ground.
The Moon orbits Earth under gravity.
keyTakeaways: Newton connected terrestrial and celestial motion.
Science builds on earlier work.
Mathematical models must be tested.
